title: The rich Stoic
hookLine: critics then and now point out that Seneca preached simplicity while very wealthy (On the Happy Life 17)

lines: BREAD AND WATER ARE ENOUGH, HE SAID.
cards: For about sixty days, a man has been telling us that bread and water are enough, that the parade of silver is only a show, that gold ceilings hide a dusty soul. Here's what he owned. Country estates.

Gardens near Rome. Loans across the empire, his critics said. One accuser, as Tacitus reports, put his gains in the hundreds of millions of sesterces, a sum hard to translate into anything we'd recognize.
Five days ago we promised to look at this honestly. Seneca, to his credit, looks at it too.

teach.b: First, the critics, then. Tacitus reports that a senator named Suillius attacked Seneca in public: how had this philosopher gathered three hundred million sesterces in four years of royal friendship?
Through lending, Suillius said, that drained Italy and the provinces. A much later historian, Cassius Dio, even blames Seneca's loans in Britain for stirring up a revolt there.
Historians argue over how far to trust either accuser: Suillius was settling scores, and Dio is often hostile. Second, Seneca's own book.
In On the Happy Life he puts the charge in his critics' mouths himself: why do you talk one way and live another? You praise poverty and keep estates. You praise simplicity and serve fine wine.
He doesn't skip the question. Third, his answer. A wise person, he argues, isn't forbidden wealth; the wealth simply mustn't own the person.

teach.h: IN THE HOUSE, NOT IN THE HEART.
teach.b: Riches should sit in the house, not in the heart. If they vanished, the wise person would lose things, not themselves. Fourth, minding the gap.
Is that a fair answer or a convenient one? Readers have argued about it ever since, and this path won't settle it.

teach.h: THE QUESTION ANYONE CAN BE ASKED.
teach.b: What's useful is the shape of the problem: anyone who names a value can be asked Seneca's question.
He at least wrote the accusation down in his own book, where every reader could see it.

how: Some readers of Seneca wrestle openly with his wealth, using the tension to examine the gaps between their own stated values and their daily lives.

games.q: you're Seneca, and critics say you praise poverty while living in luxury. what do you write?
o: state the charge plainly and argue riches belong in the house, not the heart.
games.why: he puts the accusation in his own book and answers it, an answer readers still argue over.

practice: Pick one thing you say you value, patience, honesty, simple living, and look gently at last week: where did your life match it, and where didn't it?
Don't build a case against yourself or a defense; just see the gap like the distance between two stepping stones, and ask what one step would close it by a few inches.
